gaps.sentence: My uncle, ___ lives in Canada, is coming to stay next week.
gaps.hint: non-defining clause after a comma about a person
gaps.explanation: In non-defining clauses (between commas) 'that' is not allowed; 'who' refers to people.

gaps.sentence: The police have arrested the man ___ stole the painting.
gaps.explanation: 'Who' is the subject relative pronoun for people in defining clauses.

gaps.sentence: He passed all his exams first time, ___ surprised everyone.
gaps.hint: refers to the whole previous clause
gaps.explanation: 'Which' can refer to a whole idea ('he passed first time'); this non-defining use never takes 'that'.

gaps.sentence: They chose a guide on ___ they could rely completely.
gaps.hint: rely on somebody — person after preposition
gaps.explanation: After the preposition 'on', the person takes 'whom'; 'which' is only for things.

gaps.sentence: It was the best meal ___ I have ever eaten.
gaps.hint: after a superlative, this pronoun is preferred
gaps.explanation: After superlatives ('the best ...'), 'that' is the preferred relative pronoun in defining clauses.

gaps.sentence: The programme ___ I watched last night was about volcanoes.
gaps.explanation: 'Which' refers to things, even when it is the object of the clause.

gaps.sentence: The country is in a situation ___ an election seems inevitable.
gaps.explanation: 'Where' is used with abstract nouns like situation, case and point; 'which' cannot introduce the clause here.

gaps.sentence: The train ___ leaves at six is usually very crowded.
gaps.explanation: 'Which' is the subject pronoun for things; the clause sits between the subject 'train' and its verb 'is'.
